phases.name: Fix remediation_runner sweeping up build approvals
phases.description: Bug, confirmed live 2026-07-28: core/remediation_runner.py get_approved() ("[r for r in load_requests() if r.get('status') == 'approved']") returns every status=="approved" record from memory/approval_queue.json with no filter -- including build architecture/deploy approvals created by core.approval.create_build_approval (build_id/phase_id/approval_type set, incident=None), not just genuine incident-remediation approvals created by core.approval.create_request (incident_id set, no build_id). Build 13G's own architecture-approval request got swept into process()'s Docker-remediation execution loop this way: treated approve_architecture as a container action (harmlessly rejected as status: "blocked" by docker_actions.execute_action since it is not in ALLOWED_ACTIONS, no real container was touched), then mark_executed() unconditionally flipped it to "executed" with a bogus remediation record attached -- silently corrupting approval-queue history for every build/deploy approval, not just this one, and this record's "executed" status is misleading (a build architecture approval is never "executed" the way a Docker remediation is). Fix: get_approved() must exclude any request with a build_id set (the field only create_build_approval ever sets, and the natural, already-existing discriminator between the two request shapes) so only genuine incident-remediation requests ever reach process()/execute_action.

phases.name: Scheduler: periodic systemd watchdog ping during long build cycles
phases.description: Bug, confirmed live 2026-07-28: core/scheduler.py's start() loop only calls notify("WATCHDOG=1") once, after run_cycle() returns -- but run_cycle() -> advance_builds() -> _run_generation() blocks synchronously on a single opencode/claude coding-agent subprocess call that can legitimately run many minutes. When that exceeds the systemd unit's WatchdogSec (currently 600s, set in /etc/systemd/system/ai-orchestrator.service.d/override.conf -- outside this repo, not something this phase touches), systemd SIGABRTs the whole service mid-generation. Observed live: build 13G's first generation attempt was killed this way after ~9 minutes, the service auto-restarted (Restart=always), and the new scheduler cycle immediately re-ran generation on the same still-GENERATING build from scratch (a second opencode run against a workspace that already had partial commits from the killed attempt) -- wasteful and confusing, though not data-corrupting since the workspace is an isolated clone. Fix: ping the watchdog periodically *during* a cycle, not just after it completes, so a long-but-still-alive generation call doesn't look indistinguishable from a hang to systemd. A background thread started at the top of the while loop's iteration (before calling run_cycle()) that calls notify("WATCHDOG=1") on a fixed interval well under WatchdogSec (e.g. every 30-60s), stopped once run_cycle() returns, is the natural fix -- no change to run_cycle()/build_manager/ai_router needed, this is purely scheduler.py's own heartbeat granularity.
completion_criteria: scheduler.py pings WATCHDOG=1 on a fixed interval (well under the systemd unit's WatchdogSec) throughout a cycle's execution, not only once after run_cycle() returns
The periodic ping stops cleanly once the cycle completes or the process is shutting down -- no leaked background thread across loop iterations
No change to run_cycle(), build_manager.py, or ai_router.py -- fix is contained to scheduler.py
New test (or documented manual verification note, if systemd/notify can't be meaningfully unit-tested) covers that the heartbeat mechanism starts and stops correctly around a cycle

Fix needs two parts working together: (1) build/workspace creation gives a self-modifying build access to both repos when its work needs the plugin -- e.g. _create_isolated_self_clone() also clones ai-orchestrator-plugin as a sibling directory inside the same workspace root, so a single --dir covers both trees; (2) deploy_build()'s self-modifying path merges each repo's branch back into its own live origin (SELF_PROJECT_PATH and the plugin's own live path) rather than assuming one repo -- a merge conflict or failure in either repo should fail the whole deploy, not partially apply. Phases that never touch the plugin should see no behavior change (single-repo clone/merge exactly as today) -- this should be additive, not a rewrite of the whole self-build path.

phases.description: Implements the already-approved design at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-parallel-build-execution-design.md (Status: Approved, not yet implemented) -- follow it directly rather than re-deriving the approach, it has full code sketches for every part below. High-impact, significant improvement to overall throughput: today build_manager.advance_builds() is a plain sequential for loop (confirmed live 2026-07-28) -- one build advances per scheduler cycle regardless of how many are ready, so every other queued roadmap phase waits in a single file behind whichever build is currently running. Four parts: (1) advance_builds() dispatches every ready build (REQUESTED/PLANNING/GENERATING/CODE_REVIEW/DEPLOYING) into a ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_concurrent_builds, default 2 from config/providers.yaml), each worker calling the existing _run_planning/_run_generation/_run_deployment functions unchanged -- single-build behavior stays exactly as today when there's only one ready build; (2) a new core.memory.update(name, mutate_fn) primitive (core/memory.py + core/memory_manager.py), reusing the existing fcntl.flock critical section, so read-modify-write state changes are atomic across threads and processes -- core.ai.ai_router._rotate_candidates (still a non-atomic load-then-save today, confirmed live) is rewritten on top of it, closing the race where two concurrently-dispatched builds could land on the same starting provider; _persist_build() likewise updates one build's record by id instead of resaving the whole list; (3) a new CODE_REVIEW build state between GENERATING and SECURITY_REVIEW -- an automated, purely advisory Claude review of non-Claude-generated builds' diffs (skipped when generated_by == 'claude', since there's no value in Claude reviewing its own work; skipped gracefully if Claude is unavailable) -- never auto-approves or auto-blocks, existing human approval gates are untouched; (4) a GENERATION_DISCIPLINE_PREAMBLE prepended to every generation instruction so every provider is held to the same 'write tests, run them, verify before claiming done' standard this project's own workflow follows.
completion_criteria: advance_builds() runs multiple ready builds concurrently via ThreadPoolExecutor, capped at max_concurrent_builds
Single-ready-build behavior (the common case today) is unchanged -- no regression for sequential operation
core.memory.update() is atomic (fcntl.flock-based) and _rotate_candidates/_persist_build use it, closing the read-then-write race
New CODE_REVIEW state: Claude reviews non-Claude-generated builds only, never auto-approves/blocks, degrades gracefully if Claude is unavailable
GENERATION_DISCIPLINE_PREAMBLE applied to every generation instruction regardless of provider
Full test list from the design doc's Testing section is implemented and passing

phases.name: Dual-repo deploy rollback must not discard unrelated uncommitted changes
phases.description: Gap found live 2026-07-29 during manual review of 13Q's deploy (build 18488584), before approving: core.deployment_manager._merge_self_modifying_build's dual-repo rollback path (added by 13Q) reacts to a second-repo (plugin) merge failure by running `git reset --hard <pre_merge_head>` on every already-merged live repo, including SELF_PROJECT_PATH -- this project's own live working directory. Unlike the pre-13Q single-repo failure path (`git merge --abort`, which only undoes the merge attempt itself and leaves any other uncommitted working-tree state untouched), `git reset --hard` unconditionally discards ALL uncommitted changes in the working tree at that moment, not just the merge commit being rolled back. Confirmed live: at the moment of this review, `git status` on SELF_PROJECT_PATH showed an uncommitted roadmap.json change (routine autonomous status-sync churn) -- had a dual-repo deploy been running then and failed on the plugin-repo merge, that uncommitted change would have been silently destroyed as collateral damage of rolling back a merge that had nothing to do with it. Confirmed via tests/test_deployment_manager.py (13Q's own new tests): rollback tests only assert the merge itself is cleanly undone, none set up pre-existing uncommitted changes before triggering the second-repo failure path, so this gap has zero test coverage in either direction. This gap is currently inert (requires a dual-repo deploy to actually run and fail on its second repo, which has not happened yet in production), but must be fixed before 13Q's dual-repo path is ever exercised for real against a phase that touches the plugin. Fix: before performing any merge in _merge_self_modifying_build, capture whether the live repo's working tree is dirty (git status --porcelain) with enough information to restore it (e.g. git stash create/store, or refuse the whole deploy upfront if the live repo already has uncommitted changes, forcing a human to resolve that first) -- reset --hard on rollback must restore exactly the state that existed before this deploy attempt started, not silently discard whatever a human or another process had in progress in the live tree at the time.
completion_criteria: A dual-repo deploy that fails on its second repo's merge restores each already-merged live repo to its exact pre-deploy state, including any uncommitted working-tree changes that existed before the deploy attempt started -- not just the merge commit

Alternative acceptable approach: deploy_build() refuses to start a self-modifying deploy at all (fails fast with a clear reason) if the target live repo's working tree is already dirty, rather than risking destructive rollback later
The existing single-repo failure path (git merge --abort) is unaffected -- this only closes the gap introduced by 13Q's dual-repo rollback path

New tests cover: a dual-repo deploy that fails on the second repo, with pre-existing uncommitted changes present in the live orchestrator repo beforehand, ends with those changes intact (or the deploy is refused upfront, per whichever approach is chosen)

phases.name: Kai platform auth foundation: local accounts + capability-based permissions
phases.description: Foundation for the 'Kai Enterprise Platform' initiative (user proposal 2026-07-29, trimmed after review). Scope, deliberately narrow: local username/password accounts (no external OAuth) plus a capability-based permission check -- capabilities like deploy.build, approve.architecture, chat.use, roadmap.create, provider.configure, each independently checkable in code -- mapped to exactly two initial roles: 'operator' (every capability, i.e. what the single existing bridge-token operator already has today) and 'viewer' (read-only: dashboard/chat reads, no write capabilities). Capability checks must live in one shared module (e.g. core/authz.py) that every write endpoint in core/api.py calls, not duplicated per-endpoint logic. Explicitly deferred from the original proposal, and why: full OAuth (Google/Microsoft/GitHub) + MFA + service accounts was scoped for a system with exactly one real user today -- add a second auth provider only when a real second person needs one, not speculatively. A 6-role taxonomy (Owner/Architect/Developer/Analyst/Customer/Guest) was cut to 2 roles for the same reason -- the capability model means adding a narrower role later is a mapping change, not a redesign, so there is no lock-in cost to starting minimal. The 'Customer' role scoped to assigned projects implied a multi-tenant customer-facing product pivot that was never a stated goal -- if that direction is wanted later it needs its own explicit decision, not a permissions bullet. Multi-organization support (isolated users/projects/learning/providers per org) was cut entirely: there is one organization. None of these are permanently ruled out, just not built until a real need exists -- a future roadmap phase should re-propose them with a concrete driving need, not reintroduce them speculatively. Explicitly low priority and deferred (user directive 2026-07-30): multi-user work should not be picked up ahead of any single-user-focused work still pending.
completion_criteria: core/authz.py (or equivalent) defines named capabilities and a single check_capability(operator, capability) function used by every write endpoint in core/api.py
Local account storage (username + hashed password) exists; login issues a session/token distinct from the existing bridge token
Exactly two roles exist ('operator', 'viewer') each mapping to a fixed capability set; the existing bridge-token operator continues to work unchanged with full ('operator') capabilities
A 'viewer'-role account can read dashboard/chat endpoints but is rejected (403, not silently ignored) on any write endpoint
No OAuth provider integration, no MFA, no service accounts, no additional roles beyond the two above, no multi-org support -- explicitly out of scope for this phase
Tests cover: operator retains full access, viewer is rejected on every write capability, a capability check with no matching role denies by default (fail closed)
phases.note: Deferred 2026-07-30 per user directive: multi-user/enterprise features (15A-15H) are explicitly out of scope until the single-user Kai chat experience (13X, 16A) is complete and proven. Kai has exactly one operator for now. Revisit this whole phase group after 13X/16A/13H ship -- do not spend build effort preparing for multiple users before then.

phases.name: Self-modification guardrail: mandatory review for auth/security-critical code
phases.description: Direct consequence of adding 15A's multi-user auth: once more than one identity can request builds, a self-modifying build touching authz/RBAC/credential-handling code (core/authz.py, account storage, core/security.py, provider credential loading, the API token/bridge-token mechanism itself) must never be treated like an ordinary code change -- a 'viewer'-capability user asking Kai to 'fix a bug' in core/authz.py must not be able to quietly widen their own or anyone else's permissions and sail through the normal architecture-approval flow unnoticed. Add a fixed, explicit path/module allowlist (auth/RBAC/credential files) checked in build_manager._run_planning or _create_architecture_approval: when a plan's generated diff touches any listed path, the architecture-approval request is flagged (distinct risk marker, e.g. risk='security-critical') and requires the 'operator' role specifically -- never auto-approved by any lower-privileged automation, regardless of who originally requested the build. This mirrors the existing core/kai/policies.py pattern (grep-enforced restriction that Kai itself can never call approve_architecture/approve_deploy) but for a different boundary: which class of change requires the highest-privilege human, not whether Kai can self-approve at all.
completion_criteria: A fixed path allowlist for auth/RBAC/credential-handling files exists in one place (not scattered)
A build whose generated diff touches any allowlisted path is flagged risk='security-critical' on its deploy/architecture approval request
A security-critical approval request can only be approved by an account with full ('operator') capabilities -- rejected if attempted by any other role, with a clear error, not a silent no-op

Tests cover: a diff touching an allowlisted file is flagged and blocked for a non-operator approver; a diff touching only unrelated files is unaffected; the allowlist check does not regress any existing architecture/deploy approval behavior for non-security-critical builds

phases.name: Kai platform audit log
phases.description: Aggregation layer, not new infrastructure: memory/build_history.json, memory/approval_queue.json's history[] entries, memory/decision_history.json, and memory/incidents.json already capture most of what an audit log needs (action, timestamp, status, operator/approved_by where set). This phase adds a single read endpoint (GET /audit) that merges these existing sources into one chronological, filterable view (by user, action type, project, date range) with CSV/JSON export -- explicitly not a new logging system or a new place actions get recorded. Device/IP capture requires 15A's session mechanism to exist first (the current single bridge-token model has no per-request client identity to log).
completion_criteria: GET /audit merges existing build/approval/decision/incident history into one chronological feed, no duplicate storage of data that already exists elsewhere
Supports filtering by user, action type, and date range; supports CSV and JSON export
Records the authenticated user (from 15A) and source IP on every write endpoint going forward, surfaced in the merged feed
Read-only for all roles including 'viewer' -- an audit log editable by any user defeats its purpose
Tests cover: a build approval, a deploy approval, and an incident all appear correctly attributed in the merged feed; filtering and export produce correct subsets

phases.name: Real-time update infrastructure for the Kai dashboard
phases.description: Everything the dashboard reads today is pull/poll-based (plain GET endpoints, no push). The original proposal's 'dashboard must update in near real-time' is its own sub-project, not a checkbox on 15E -- this phase decides and implements the actual mechanism (Server-Sent Events is the natural fit: one-way server-to-browser push, no new bidirectional protocol needed, works through the existing CloudCLI plugin proxy) and defines exactly which state changes trigger a push (build status transitions, new approval requests, roadmap phase completions) versus what stays poll-on-tab-open (static/rarely-changing data). Reuses existing state -- this phase adds a push transport on top of data that's already computed elsewhere, it does not recompute anything new.
completion_criteria: One documented push mechanism (SSE) is implemented and exposed via a new endpoint (e.g. GET /events)
A defined, minimal list of triggering state changes (build status transition, new pending approval, roadmap phase completion) push an event within a few seconds of occurring
Falls back gracefully to the existing poll-based behavior if the push connection drops -- no dashboard functionality regresses if SSE is unavailable
Tests cover: a build status transition produces a push event with correct payload; a dropped connection does not crash the dashboard or lose state on reconnect

phases.name: Kai Enterprise Dashboard: consolidate system health, provider health, usage, and notifications
phases.description: Extends 13G's Kai Dashboard and 13J's AI Workforce & Build Scheduler Dashboard rather than replacing them -- adds the remaining panels from the original proposal that don't already exist: system health summary, provider health (already partly surfaced via /providers/dashboard, needs a dedicated panel), usage statistics, and a notifications panel (surfacing anything currently requiring human attention -- pending approvals, WAITING_FOR_USER_INPUT builds -- as the visual equivalent of the Telegram alerts 13Z sends). Reuses 15D's push infrastructure for live updates rather than polling. Reuses existing APIs throughout (/health, /incidents, /decisions, /approvals, /learning, /roadmap/progress, /providers/dashboard) -- no new data computation, purely presentation and layout.
completion_criteria: Dashboard shows: system health, roadmap progress, active builds, pending approvals, build history, learning summary, provider health, usage statistics, notifications, scheduler status, Telegram status, API status -- each backed by an existing endpoint, none newly computed
Updates live via 15D's push mechanism, not full-page polling
No duplicate panel/functionality already present in 13G's Kai Dashboard or 13J's workforce dashboard -- extends them, does not fork a competing dashboard
Read access respects 15A roles ('viewer' can see it, cannot trigger any action from it)

phases.name: Kai Chat: multi-user, project-aware, conversation history
phases.description: Extends 13X's POST /kai/chat rather than replacing it. Adds: persisted conversation history per authenticated user (15A), project-aware context (conversations scoped to a project once multi-project workspaces exist -- see 15H), markdown/code-block rendering on the frontend, streaming responses, and conversation search. Every constraint 13X already established stays load-bearing and unchanged here: chat is a UI surface for an authenticated human to act through, never a new autonomous action path -- an approval-intent expressed in chat still resolves through core.approval.approve()/reject() with the real authenticated user attributed as operator, and tests/test_kai_identity.py's grep-based restriction (no approve_architecture/approve_deploy call anywhere under core/kai/) must still pass. A 'viewer'-role user can chat and ask questions but any approval/deploy intent expressed in chat is rejected by 15A's capability check exactly as it would be via the API directly -- chat must not become a side channel around the permission system.
completion_criteria: Conversation history persists per authenticated user and is retrievable/searchable
Streaming responses work end to end (backend to frontend)
Markdown and code blocks render correctly in the frontend
An approval/deploy intent expressed in chat by a 'viewer'-role account is rejected via the same 15A capability check as the direct API, not silently allowed
tests/test_kai_identity.py's existing restriction still passes unchanged
File upload is deferred to a later phase if not already trivial given the existing chat transport -- do not block this phase's completion on image/file support

phases.name: AI Workforce Center: dedicated per-worker view
phases.description: The Kai Control Center tab (13G's build, plugin repo commit a873340) already has a renderKaiDelegatedTasksCard summarizing per-provider delegation counts and success rates. This phase promotes that into a dedicated page/tab with the full per-worker detail the original proposal asked for: name, role (planning/coding/review/documentation/testing), provider, model, health, availability, current task, queue length, success rate, failure rate, average completion time. Sourced from existing provider-rotation/quota data (core/ai_provider.py, memory/provider_rotation.json, memory/ai_usage_history.json) -- no new tracking infrastructure. New providers/models must appear automatically as they're used, without a UI code change, matching how provider rotation itself already works without hardcoded provider lists.
completion_criteria: Dedicated view lists every provider/model that has been delegated to at least once, with all fields from the description
A newly-used provider/model appears automatically on next data refresh with no UI code change required
Queue length and current-task fields reflect real in-flight state, not stale/cached data
Data is sourced entirely from existing provider-rotation/usage records -- no duplicate tracking added

phases.name: Multi-project workspaces
phases.description: Support more than one project inside Kai, each with its own conversations (15F), roadmap, builds, documentation, learning, approvals, and deployments, switchable without leaving the chat/dashboard. This is scoped to multiple projects for the single existing operator -- not multi-tenancy and not multi-organization (15A's deferred-scope note applies here too: isolating data between organizations is a separate, not-yet-justified phase). Existing self-modifying-build machinery (core.roadmap_manager's SELF_PROJECT_PATH handling) must remain a distinct, special-cased project -- ordinary projects use the existing isolated-clone/template flow (core/project_templates.py, core/repo_manager.py) unchanged, this phase only adds the ability to hold several of them and switch context between them. Explicitly low priority and deferred (user directive 2026-07-30): multi-user work should not be picked up ahead of any single-user-focused work still pending.
completion_criteria: A user can create/switch between multiple projects without a new login or losing chat context
Each project's conversations, roadmap, builds, and approvals are isolated from every other project's
The self-modifying ai-orchestrator project itself continues to work exactly as today -- not folded into the generic multi-project mechanism in a way that risks its special-cased handling
Tests cover: switching projects returns the correct isolated data for each; no cross-project data leakage in any listing endpoint

phases.name: Standalone Kai dashboard, decoupled from CloudCLI's lifecycle
phases.description: Confirmed live 2026-07-30: the only existing Kai UI (13G's Kai Control Center) is embedded as a CloudCLI plugin tab -- it inherits CloudCLI's own hosting, auth, and lifecycle. The user hit this directly: the dashboard showed 'Failed to load: RPC error 404' coinciding with a routine ai-orchestrator-api.service restart, and separately CloudCLI itself had an unrelated host-level update prompt that looked related but wasn't. Kai and CloudCLI are conceptually separate systems; the dashboard should not go down because the other one is restarting, updating, or simply not running. Add a standalone dashboard: a small static HTML/JS page served directly by core.api (e.g. GET /dashboard) at its own URL, reachable independent of CloudCLI entirely. Reuses every existing read endpoint as-is (/health, /roadmap/progress, /approvals, /providers/dashboard, /learning, /builds) -- no new backend logic, this is presentation only. Deliberately READ-ONLY for this phase: core.api's GET endpoints require no auth today (only POST/write endpoints check the bridge token), so a browser-servable page can safely call them directly -- but embedding the bridge token itself into browser-facing JS to support write actions (approve/reject) would leak it to anyone who can load the page, bypassing CloudCLI's proxy entirely. Approve/reject actions stay on the existing CloudCLI-embedded tab until 15A's real auth exists; this phase does not attempt to solve write-auth early.
completion_criteria: GET /dashboard (or similar) serves a self-contained HTML/JS page directly from core.api, reachable without CloudCLI running

Page displays system health, roadmap progress, active builds, pending approvals (read-only display, no action buttons), provider health/cost, and learning summary -- reusing existing GET endpoints only, no new data computation
No write/approve/reject actions on this page, and no bridge token embedded in any browser-servable file -- explicitly deferred to 15A
Page continues to load and display data correctly with CloudCLI's cloudcli.service stopped (proves the decoupling)
Tests cover: the route serves valid HTML, and a smoke test confirms it doesn't import/require anything from the CloudCLI plugin bridge
phases.note: Re-prioritized 2026-07-30 per user directive: pulled forward from Phase 16 to sit right behind 13X. Only dependency is 13G (already complete), so it can build in parallel with or immediately after 13X. Still read-only per its original scope -- write actions stay on the existing embedded tab until real auth exists, which is fine since multi-user auth (15A) is deferred, not needed for this decision.

phases.name: Self-healing: automated recovery for known, scoped failure classes
phases.description: Follow-on to 14A's stuck-phase detection -- detection alone still requires a human (or this session) to notice and act. For a narrow, already-evidenced set of failure classes seen live this session, attempt automatic recovery before ever paging a human: (1) a build stuck oscillating between WAITING_FOR_USER_INPUT and PLANNING with no real open question (14A's own detection target) -- auto-resubmit a nudge answer once, then escalate if it recurs; (2) a generation/deploy attempt that failed on a now-understood, already-fixed infra bug class (dirty working tree, missing memory/ snapshot, no-op generation) -- these are exactly the failure signatures this session spent tonight fixing at the root, so recovery here means confirming the fix landed and safely retrying, not re-deriving new logic; (3) the orchestrator/API systemd services themselves -- confirm systemd's own Restart= policy is actually configured (verify, don't assume) and add a lightweight liveness self-check the scheduler cycle already has the means to perform. Deliberately NOT in scope: certificate expiry, disk-space monitoring, or any other failure class with no live evidence it's a real risk on this single-host deployment -- added speculatively, they'd be untested guesses. Every auto-recovery action must be logged (what failed, what recovery was attempted, outcome) and still notify a human via 13Z's Telegram bridge if the automated attempt doesn't resolve it -- 'notify humans only when autonomous recovery is unsuccessful' is the exact behavior, not silent-always or loud-always.
completion_criteria: A build stuck oscillating WAITING_FOR_USER_INPUT/PLANNING (14A's detection) gets one automated recovery attempt before human escalation
systemd Restart= policy for ai-orchestrator.service and ai-orchestrator-api.service is verified/confirmed configured correctly (or fixed if it isn't) -- not assumed
Every auto-recovery attempt (trigger, action taken, outcome) is logged to a queryable record, not just console/log-file text
Telegram notification (via 13Z) fires only when an automated recovery attempt fails or a failure class isn't recognized -- never spams on successful auto-recovery
Explicitly does not add certificate/disk-space/other speculative monitoring with no live evidence of being a real risk here
Tests cover: the two evidenced failure classes trigger correct recovery attempts, and an unrecognized failure class correctly falls through to human notification rather than being silently swallowed

phases.name: Continuous self-improvement: scheduled analysis answering concrete questions from real data
phases.description: Kai already has the mechanism to propose new roadmap phases from its own observations (13I, add_phase() defaulting to status='proposed' so a human must promote it -- 'AI can propose, AI cannot approve its own changes' stays true). This phase is the analysis engine that actually generates those proposals on a schedule, answering concrete questions from data that already exists rather than speculating: which provider/model actually performs best per role (reuses 13T's provider_evidence module and its MIN_SAMPLE_SIZE/relative-comparison approach, don't reinvent it), which roadmap phases failed most often and why (memory/build_history.json + roadmap.json's own 'note' fields, several of which already document real root causes from tonight), which tests are flaky (repeated CI-adjacent failures with no code change between runs -- needs evidence across multiple self-build test-gate runs, not a guess), and where token/cost is being wasted (13W's now-real per-call cost data, ai_usage_history.json). Each answered question that surfaces a genuine, evidenced improvement becomes one 13I-style proposed phase, never auto-promoted to pending. Explicitly not in scope: fabricating an answer when the underlying data doesn't support one (13T's own MIN_SAMPLE_SIZE discipline applies here too -- 'insufficient data' is a valid, honest output).
completion_criteria: A scheduled (or Kai-command-triggered) analysis run answers each of: best-performing provider per role, most-failed roadmap phases + root cause pattern, flaky tests (if any evidenced), and token/cost waste hotspots
Every proposal it files goes through roadmap_engine.add_phase() with status='proposed', never 'pending' -- reuses 13I's existing mechanism, does not add a second proposal pathway
An analysis question with insufficient supporting data reports 'insufficient data' rather than fabricating a recommendation, matching 13T's established sample-size discipline
Reuses core.ai.provider_evidence (13T) and the real cost data (13W) directly -- no duplicate data collection
Tests cover: a well-evidenced finding produces a correctly-shaped proposed phase, and a question with too little data correctly abstains rather than guessing

phases.name: Cost budget limits and alerts on top of 13W's real cost data
phases.description: Small, direct follow-on to 13W (completed 2026-07-29): real per-call cost is now captured in ai_usage_history.json and aggregated per-provider via get_provider_dashboard() when a provider's response actually reports a figure. This phase adds the alerting layer on top of data that already exists -- no new cost tracking, purely thresholds and notification. A configurable budget limit (e.g. daily/monthly spend ceiling, overall or per-provider) checked against the existing aggregated totals; crossing it sends a Telegram alert (via 13Z) with the actual figures, not a vague warning. No automatic spend-limiting/provider-disabling behavior in this phase -- alert-only, since automatically cutting off a provider mid-roadmap based on a cost threshold is a judgment call for a human, not something to automate without being asked.
completion_criteria: A configurable budget limit (at least a total daily/monthly ceiling) is checked against 13W's existing real cost aggregates -- no new cost computation
Crossing the limit sends a Telegram alert via 13Z's bridge with the actual spend figures, not a generic message
No automatic provider-disabling or spend-limiting action taken -- alert only, this phase does not make autonomous spending decisions
Tests cover: an alert fires exactly once when a threshold is crossed (not every cycle after), and stays silent under the threshold

phases.name: Parallel self-build execution: serialize only the merge step, not the whole phase
phases.description: Discovered live 2026-07-30 while investigating why 16A ran before the newly-reprioritized 13X: core.roadmap_manager.advance_roadmap() hard-limits self-modifying builds to exactly one phase in flight at a time, with a comment justifying this by builds sharing SELF_PROJECT_PATH's live working directory -- but that rationale is stale. K3 (completed) already gives every self-build its own isolated clone (_create_isolated_self_clone(), under ~/.ai-orchestrator/self-build-workspaces/), so planning, generation, code review, and security review for multiple phases can safely run concurrently today -- each operates entirely inside its own clone. The one real shared resource is the final merge into the live repo (core.deployment_manager._merge_branch_into_live_repo()) during DEPLOYING, which must still happen one at a time to avoid two builds racing on the same git HEAD. This phase relaxes advance_roadmap()'s single-in-flight check to only serialize the merge/deploy step (e.g. a merge lock or queue), letting build_manager.advance_builds()'s existing MAX_CONCURRENT_BUILDS-based thread pool actually parallelize the earlier lifecycle stages for self-modifying phases the way it already does for regular app builds. Must also handle a build going stale relative to another build that merged first while it was still generating -- e.g. re-checking for merge conflicts and re-running tests against the latest live HEAD immediately before merge, not trusting a plan/generation that ran against an now-outdated base.
completion_criteria: Two self-modifying phases can be in PLANNING/GENERATING/CODE_REVIEW/SECURITY_REVIEW simultaneously, each in its own isolated clone
Only one build merges into the live repo at a time -- concurrent merge attempts are queued/locked, never racing on the same HEAD

A build whose isolated clone has fallen behind live HEAD (because another phase merged first) is detected and safely re-tested/re-merged against the current HEAD, not blindly merged against a stale base
The existing single-phase-in-flight safety this replaces is not silently dropped for builds that still need true isolation (e.g. still serialize if a build is proven unsafe to run concurrently)
Tests cover: two phases advancing in parallel, a merge-time conflict between two concurrently-completed phases, and a build correctly detecting/handling a stale base at merge time
phases.note: Queued 2026-07-30 per user request, deliberately low priority -- this is a throughput/efficiency improvement, not a blocker for the current top priority (13X/16A/13H, direct Kai chat). Revisit after those ship.

phases.name: Wire a chat panel into the CloudCLI-embedded Kai Control Center tab, calling POST /kai/chat
phases.description: Direct follow-on to 13X (POST /kai/chat) -- shipping the backend endpoint alone leaves nowhere safe to actually type into it. The standalone dashboard (16A) deliberately does not hold the bridge token (embedding it in browser JS would leak it to anyone who loads the page, since there is no per-user auth yet -- write auth is explicitly deferred to 15A), so it cannot call 13X's endpoint on its own. The existing CloudCLI-embedded Kai Control Center tab (13G, completed, /project/src/ai-orchestrator-plugin) already has a server-side Node.js proxy (dist/server.js) that holds the bridge token securely and proxies authenticated write calls on the operator's behalf -- the same pattern already used for the tab's existing Approve/Reject buttons. Add a simple chat panel to that tab: a text input, a send button, and a scrolling message history, POSTing through the plugin's existing server-side proxy to POST /kai/chat (never embedding the bridge token client-side). This is the concrete answer to "where do I actually type to Kai" -- reliability over visual polish, per the user's explicit MVP framing for the chat experience.
completion_criteria: A chat panel (input box, send button, scrolling history) exists in the Kai Control Center tab
Messages route through the plugin's existing server-side bridge-token proxy -- the token is never sent to or embedded in browser-facing code
Conversation history displayed in the panel matches what POST /kai/chat persists (13X's memory/kai_chat_history.json)
Sending a message and receiving a real, non-fabricated response works end to end against a running backend
No new approval mechanism and no write capability added beyond what already existed in the tab -- this only adds a transport for 13X's existing endpoint
phases.note: Queued 2026-07-30 per user request, immediately after 13X in priority -- this closes the gap between "the chat backend exists" and "I can actually open something and type to Kai," which is the exact milestone the user has been asking for.

phases.name: Restart ai-orchestrator-api.service after a self-modifying deploy actually merges
phases.description: Confirmed live 2026-07-30: 17B merged GET /kai/chat into core/api.py cleanly (commit visible in the live repo, tests passed) but the running ai-orchestrator-api.service process had been up since 04:25 that morning -- Python does not hot-reload, so the new route returned a genuine 404 until manually restarted, even though the deploy itself reported COMPLETED/VERIFIED. This is systemic, not a one-off: core/deployment_manager.py has zero logic anywhere to restart the live service after a self-modifying merge -- grep for "systemctl"/"restart" in that file only turns up container crash-loop counting, unrelated to reloading the orchestrator's own process. Every future deploy that touches any module core.api or the scheduler daemon has already imported will have this same silent-stale-code problem. This likely also explains part of the earlier "Kai Control Center RPC 404" investigation (2026-07-30 briefing) that was chalked up to transient restart timing -- the real mechanism may have simply been stale-code-until-restart, recurring by coincidence rather than being a one-off blip. Fix: after a self-modifying build reaches VERIFIED/COMPLETED (post-merge, post self-build-test-suite-pass), restart ai-orchestrator-api.service (and ai-orchestrator.service if the change touched anything the scheduler daemon itself imports, not just the API layer) via systemctl. Must be graceful: only restart if the merge actually succeeded (never on a rolled-back/failed deploy), and should not restart on every deploy indiscriminately if a phase touched neither service's code (e.g. a pure roadmap.json/docs-only change) -- avoid unnecessary restarts that could drop in-flight requests for no reason. Essential, high-impact fix -- every future deploy touching live-imported code is silently broken without it. Low risk / non-breaking / backward-compatible: purely additive restart logic gated on successful merge, does not change any existing deploy behavior.
completion_criteria: A successful self-modifying deploy that changes core/api.py (or any module the running api service has imported) results in ai-orchestrator-api.service actually restarting automatically, with no manual intervention required
A deploy that only touches roadmap.json/docs/non-imported files does not trigger an unnecessary service restart
A failed/rolled-back deploy never triggers a restart
The restart is logged (what triggered it, which service, outcome) for observability
Tests cover: successful merge touching core/api.py triggers restart; roadmap-only change does not; failed merge does not restart
phases.note: Queued 2026-07-30, discovered live: 17B chat panel returned RPC 404 in production after a clean merge because the live API service was never restarted to pick up the new route. High priority -- this silently breaks every future deploy that touches live-imported code until a human happens to notice and manually restart, which is exactly the kind of gap this session has been finding and fixing all day.

phases.name: Standalone Kai Dashboard: real server-side proxy + full tabbed interface (chat, approvals, workforce, learning, roadmap)
phases.description: User directive 2026-07-30: consolidate all of Kai's interfaces (chat, approvals, AI workforce, learning, roadmap) onto the standalone dashboard (16A, GET /dashboard on core.api) as real tabs, not just the current read-only summary. 16A was deliberately read-only because the standalone page has no bridge token and the dashboard is reachable from anything on the LAN (core.api now binds 0.0.0.0, not just 127.0.0.1) -- embedding the write-capable bridge token directly in that page's browser-facing JS would let anyone on the LAN who loads the page extract it and act as the full operator (approve/reject builds, chat as the operator), not just view. User explicitly chose the safe option: give the standalone dashboard its own lightweight server-side proxy, mirroring the CloudCLI plugin's existing pattern (ai-orchestrator-plugin/src/server.ts -- a small process that holds the bridge token server-side and forwards authenticated requests on the browser's behalf, never exposing the token itself). Concretely: a new small server component (could live in core.api itself as a same-origin proxy path, or a separate lightweight process) that the dashboard's browser JS talks to instead of calling write endpoints directly -- the real bridge token never reaches the browser. Add real tab navigation to the dashboard (currently a single scrolling page) covering: Overview/health, Chat (reusing 13X/17B's POST+GET /kai/chat), Approvals (with real approve/reject actions now safely possible through the proxy), AI Workforce/providers, Learning, Roadmap. This becomes the single place with everything, without needing the CloudCLI-embedded tab at all going forward -- though that tab should keep working unchanged, not be removed by this phase.
completion_criteria: The standalone dashboard has real tab navigation (not one long scrolling page) covering Overview, Chat, Approvals, AI Workforce, Learning, and Roadmap
A server-side proxy holds the bridge token -- confirmed via test that the token never appears in any browser-servable file or API response reachable from the dashboard's own JS
Chat (send + history) works end-to-end through the standalone dashboard using this proxy, reusing 13X/17B's existing POST/GET /kai/chat -- no new chat backend logic

Approve/reject actions on the Approvals tab work end-to-end through the proxy and correctly attribute the real operator, reusing the existing core.approval.approve()/reject() calls -- no new approval mechanism
The existing CloudCLI-embedded Kai Control Center tab (13G/17B) continues to work unchanged
Tests cover: token never leaks to the browser bundle/responses, chat send+history round-trip, approve/reject through the proxy with correct operator attribution
phases.note: Queued 2026-07-30 per explicit user choice among three options -- this one keeps the same security model 16A was originally built around (no token in browser JS) rather than trading it away for speed. Essential, high-value, but not urgent-blocking -- the CloudCLI tab already has working chat today via 17B.

phases.name: Multi-node Proxmox registry + full inventory discovery (Proxmox A + B, extensible)
phases.description: User directive 2026-07-30 (trimmed from a larger charter -- multi-Proxmox management without clustering, matching the users own explicit "never cluster, treat each node independently" requirement, consistent with the earlier decision to cancel a full 14-phase enterprise buildout in favor of scoped, real needs). core.health.analyze_proxmox() already exists but is narrow -- single node (Proxmox A only, via memory/last_scan.json proxmox.node.data), CPU/memory thresholds only. This phase: (1) a node registry (e.g. memory/proxmox_nodes.json or similar, schema_version/records convention) so nodes are config-driven, not hardcoded -- Proxmox A (192.168.99.2, API token via existing proxdash credential or a dedicated one) and Proxmox B (10.8.0.102, reachable now via the WireGuard tunnel fixed 2026-07-30, API token already provided by the user -- this needs to move from floating in conversation context into the ai-orchestrator's own credential storage, not remain dependent on a human re-supplying it each session); (2) full inventory per node via the Proxmox REST API (already sufficient for everything requested -- version, CPU, RAM, storage, VMs, containers, networks, and disk/SMART health via /nodes/{node}/disks/list -- SSH is NOT required for any of this and should not be added as a second credential/attack-surface unless a concrete gap is found); (3) a simple generated topology doc (markdown + a mermaid diagram) from the live inventory, saved to /uploads or docs/, regenerable on demand not just once. Explicitly NOT in scope: cluster creation/joining (user has repeatedly and explicitly ruled this out), replication-status monitoring (no replication is configured between any nodes today -- would be permanent noise; add only once real replication exists), SSH-based management.
completion_criteria: A node registry exists, config-driven (adding a new node does not require code changes)
Proxmox A and Proxmox B both return full inventory (version, CPU, RAM, storage, VMs, CTs, networks, disk/SMART health) via their REST APIs
